article_title: Investing in Adolescents
citation: Shanette C. Porter, C. Kirabo Jackson, Sebastián Kiguel and John Q. Easton. (2023). Investing in Adolescents: High School Climate and Organizational Context Shape Student Development and Educational Attainment. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Effective high schools feature supportive environments, ambitious instruction, and collaborative teachers
description: The study identifies a pattern of school organizational characteristics shared by high schools that supported students' development on all dimensions of growth. Such schools featured "Supportive environments in which students feel safe, supported, and find teachers trustworthy and responsive to their needs", ambitious instruction with challenging, engaging, well-structured classes that build on prior knowledge, and collaborative teachers active in school improvement, committed to their school, and engaged in professional development.
requirements: Schools must combine a rigorous instructional environment with strong and supportive school-based relationships, which the release says adolescents may be particularly responsive to.
examples: The study characterized high schools supporting growth on all dimensions using 5Essentials Survey measures of school climate completed by high school students and teachers.
key_sources: Shanette C. Porter, C. Kirabo Jackson, Sebastián Kiguel and John Q. Easton. (2023). Investing in Adolescents: High School Climate and Organizational Context Shape Student Development and Educational Attainment. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/investing-in-adolescents

article_title: Coaching at Scale: A Strategy for Strengthening the Early Learning Workforce
citation: Schachner, A., Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Barajas, J. (2024). Coaching at scale: A strategy for strengthening the early learning workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/984.909
title: Effective coaching combines a strong coach-educator partnership, reflection and individualized feedback, focused observations, intentional coaching plans, and job-embedded active learning
description: The report identifies a set of research-based characteristics of effective early childhood coaching models. As the executive summary states, "effective coaching relies on a strong partnership between coaches and educators; reflection and individualized feedback; focused observations; intentional coaching plans to guide sessions; and job-embedded learning opportunities for active learning." Each feature is grounded in reviews of coaching research, with the coach-coachee relationship described as the foundation of coaching effectiveness. The principle also encompasses coach knowledge: successful coaches need knowledge of the coaching model, general coaching and consultation skills, and knowledge of child development and teaching.
requirements: Coaches with knowledge of the specific coaching model and practices, general coaching and consultation skills such as understanding adult learning principles and building rapport, and knowledge of early childhood development and teaching
constraints: The report notes coach knowledge and skills "has received much less research attention than the other areas"
target_learners: Early childhood educators (lead and assistant teachers, home-based educators, site leaders)
target_learning_goals: Implementation of evidence-based instructional practices and improved adult-child interactions
examples: The five studied coaching systems aligned coaching content to quality standards, used classroom assessment tools to inform practice, and paired coaching with other professional development efforts.
key_sources: Schachner, A., Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Barajas, J. (2024). Coaching at scale: A strategy for strengthening the early learning workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/984.909

article_title: AIED's Unfinished Mission: Centering Agency and Motivation in the Age of Effortless Bypass
citation: H. Chad Lane. (2026). AIED's Unfinished Mission: Centering Agency and Motivation in the Age of Effortless Bypass. AIED 2026, CCIS 3032, pp. 502–516. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-29791-4_38
title: The effortless bypass dilemma: general-purpose AI lets learners complete academic tasks without effort, making authentic engagement a motivation problem
description: The effortless bypass dilemma names the challenge that general-purpose AI tools can perform academic tasks across the full cognitive pipeline, so learners can complete standard homework with simple prompts outside any designed learning environment. The author characterizes it as fundamentally a motivation problem: the goal is ensuring learners choose effortful engagement when easier alternatives exist. It frames the paper's renewed AIED research agenda.
requirements: Approaches must address the underlying motivation to engage cognitively rather than simply restricting AI use, which the author argues harms only learners without access
constraints: The dilemma arises specifically with general-purpose AI usable anonymously, effortlessly, and outside designed learning environments
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners with access to general-purpose AI tools
target_learning_goals: Authentic, effortful engagement in academic tasks across domains
examples: The paper cites calculators and the internet as earlier easier paths students used to outsource homework, positioning cognitive offloading as neither new nor unique to AI
key_sources: H. Chad Lane. (2026). AIED's Unfinished Mission: Centering Agency and Motivation in the Age of Effortless Bypass. AIED 2026, CCIS 3032, pp. 502–516. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-29791-4_38

article_title: Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis
citation: Alona Strugatski, Licol Zeinfeld, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15630
title: Released codebase, prompts, and analysis scripts for human-LLM latent structure comparison
description: The article releases the computational pipeline used for its analyses: preprocessing of binary item-response matrices, factor retention, EFA fitting, and congruence-based comparison. The paper states "The full code, sample data and prompts to reproduce the analyses in the paper can be found in the GitHub repository", and the limitations section adds that the authors "have publicly released our complete codebase, prompts, and analysis scripts". The human datasets themselves are non-public, available to researchers upon request.
requirements: Non-public human response data must be obtained from the authors upon request; the release covers code, sample data, and prompts.
constraints: Using non-public datasets constrains absolute reproducibility, as the article states in its limitations.
target_learners: researchers evaluating LLMs with educational assessments
target_learning_goals: reproducible psychometric comparison of human and LLM response data
examples: The pipeline used tetrachoric correlations, Kaiser criterion and parallel analysis retention, minres oblimin EFA, and Hungarian-algorithm-matched factor congruence over 100 resampling iterations.
key_sources: Alona Strugatski, Licol Zeinfeld, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15630

article_title: The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22687
title: Efficiency-gain illusions framework: two distinct miscalibration patterns (time vs. effort) underlying AI-use decisions
description: The article proposes that decisions to use AI rest on a cost-benefit comparison requiring calibration of one's own capabilities and the tool's, and identifies two named illusions: a speedup illusion, where predicted time savings exceed actual savings, and an offloading illusion, where predicted effort reduction exceeds actual reduction. The two follow distinct mechanisms: "for time, people misjudge the efficiency of AI assistance, while for effort, they misevaluate how hard it would be to complete tasks independently." Both miscalibrations push people toward AI use and, via a carryover effect, can form an overreliance feedback loop.
requirements: Applies to cognitively simple tasks completable in under five minutes independently, as studied in the article's task set
constraints: The article states it focuses on human miscalibration rather than AI capability, and AI capabilities change over time
target_learners: Adult AI chatbot users (US adult Prolific samples)
target_learning_goals: Well-calibrated decisions about when to use AI assistance versus completing tasks independently
examples: Study 2 operationalized the illusions formally: the speedup illusion holds when predicted minus predicted-AI time exceeds actual minus actual-AI time, and the offloading illusion analogously for NASA-TLX effort ratings.
key_sources: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22687

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Efklides' MASRL model: Person level and Task×Person level interaction of metacognition, motivation and affect
description: Efklides' Metacognitive and Affective Model of Self-Regulated Learning (MASRL) distinguishes two interacting levels. The Person level (macrolevel) is top-down and goal-driven, comprising cognition, motivation, self-concept, affect, volition, metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive skills. The Task×Person level (microlevel) is bottom-up and data-driven, where metacognitive activity takes control and attention moves to task-specific mechanisms. The review calls this distinction "probably the most salient feature of the MARSL model," and states the model clarifies how metacognition, motivation and affect interact via the macro and micro levels, with four basic functions at the microlevel: cognition, metacognition, affect, and regulation of affect and effort.
requirements: Empirical support rests on studies showing interactions among metacognition, motivation and affect at the two levels
constraints: Offers a different conceptualization of top-down/bottom-up processing than Boekaerts and Corno's account
examples: Efklides created the Metacognitive Experiences Questionnaire exploring judgments and feelings about cognitive processing
key_sources: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Efklides' MASRL model: Person (macrolevel) and Task×Person (microlevel) interactions of metacognition, motivation, and affect
description: Efklides' Metacognitive and Affective Model of Self-Regulated Learning (MASRL) distinguishes two levels. The review describes that "there is the Person level-also called macrolevel-which is the most 'traditional' view of SRL and comprehends the personal characteristics of the student", operating top-down around students' goals, and a Task×Person (microlevel) that is bottom-up and data-driven, where metacognitive monitoring takes control during task execution. The model clarifies relationships among metacognition, motivation, and affect via the interaction of the two levels and offers a different top-down/bottom-up conceptualization from Boekaerts and Corno.
requirements: Empirical support requires research showing interactions among metacognition, motivation, and affect at both levels and the effects of task demands on both
constraints: The microlevel operates during task execution, the phase the review describes as having the highest cognitive load
target_learners: students performing academic tasks across domains
target_learning_goals: integration of metacognitive experiences with motivation and affect during task performance
examples: Efklides (2002) created the Metacognitive Experiences Questionnaire exploring judgments and feelings about cognitive processing
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: Executive functions predict literacy and mathematics achievements: The unique contribution of cognitive flexibility in grades 2, 4, and 6
citation: Sofia Magalhães, Luísa Carneiro, Teresa Limpo & Marisa Filipe (2020). Executive functions predict literacy and mathematics achievements: The unique contribution of cognitive flexibility in grades 2, 4, and 6. Child Neuropsychology, 26(7), 934-952. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2020.1740188
title: Three-core-component model of executive functions with higher-order components built on top
description: The article adopts the widely used framework in which executive functions are "a set of cognitive skills involved in goal-directed activities, which are crucial for the regulation of thoughts and actions". It defines "at least three separate but related core components": working memory (storing, manipulating, and processing information during a task), inhibitory control (inhibiting an automatic tendency), and cognitive flexibility (shifting between tasks or goals). Higher-order EF such as planning and fluid intelligence are built from these cores, which share a common executive attention foundation. The study uses this structure to isolate flexibility's unique contribution by controlling for the other components.
requirements: Measures must separate the core components so each can be controlled statistically when testing one component's unique contribution
constraints: The article notes some studies failed to find flexibility as a distinct component, and that flexibility may be less differentiated from working memory and inhibition in young children
key_sources: Sofia Magalhães, Luísa Carneiro, Teresa Limpo & Marisa Filipe (2020). Executive functions predict literacy and mathematics achievements: The unique contribution of cognitive flexibility in grades 2, 4, and 6. Child Neuropsychology, 26(7), 934-952. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2020.1740188

article_title: Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes
citation: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311
title: Assess and support executive function during adolescence, a period of EF plasticity with implications for identification and training
description: Because executive function remains malleable well beyond early childhood, adolescence is a strategic window for identifying EF weaknesses and delivering EF-targeted support. The article states: "Given the plastic nature of EF , especia lly over adolescence, the current ﬁndings may have practical implications for future EF identiﬁcation and training." The study's differentiated hot/cool developmental trajectories imply that identification and training efforts should be timed to the facet-specific trajectories the study documents.
requirements: Assessment batteries should distinguish hot and cool EF facets so that identification and training can target the appropriate facet at the appropriate developmental stage
target_learning_goals: executive function development supporting academic performance and psychological adjustment
examples: The study measured five EF tasks across six age groups of adolescents and linked facet-specific developmental patterns to grades and parent-rated adjustment, motivating facet-specific identification and training
key_sources: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311

article_title: Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: Results from a Rapid Review of the International Literature, Expert Review, and Stakeholder Consultation
citation: Walsh, K., Pink, E., Ayling, N., Sondergeld, A., Dallaston, E., Tournas, P., Serry, E., Trotter, S., Spanos, T., & Rogic, N. (2022). Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: Results from a rapid review of the international literature, expert review, and stakeholder consultation. International Journal of Child-Computer Interaction, 33, Article number: 100474. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijcci.2022.100474
title: Common characteristics of effective school-based prevention initiatives collated from prevention reviews
description: From hand-searched papers on effective school-based prevention (including Nation et al. 2003, a Cochrane review of the WHO Health Promoting Schools Framework, an implementation scoping review, and WHO INSPIRE), the authors collated a set of themes conceptualised as common characteristics of effective prevention initiatives. These include a whole school approach, knowledgeable and well-trained teachers, leadership support, parent and community engagement, clear goals, effective monitoring and evaluation, developmentally and socio-culturally appropriate learning, varied and highly engaging teaching styles, positive teacher role modelling, avoiding scare tactics and confrontational strategies, and adequate duration, frequency, and intensity.
requirements: Characteristics presuppose school-based prevention delivery with trained teachers and leadership support
constraints: Collated from general school-based prevention literature; the authors note a paucity of literature on comprehensive school-based online safety education specifically
target_learning_goals: Prevention of online harms and related risk behaviours
examples: The Stage 1 rapid review captured one review detailing characteristics of effective school-based prevention initiatives (PSHE Association, 2016) and identified four further papers via hand-searching of reference lists
key_sources: Walsh, K., Pink, E., Ayling, N., Sondergeld, A., Dallaston, E., Tournas, P., Serry, E., Trotter, S., Spanos, T., & Rogic, N. (2022). Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: Results from a rapid review of the international literature, expert review, and stakeholder consultation. International Journal of Child-Computer Interaction, 33, Article number: 100474. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijcci.2022.100474

article_title: Teaching metacognitive strategies that address executive function processes within a schoolwide curriculum
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Executive function as an umbrella term for goal-directed cognitive processes
description: The volume's framing chapter defines executive function as an umbrella construct covering the cognitive processes serving goal-directed behavior. It states that "most of the definitions of executive function include many, but not all, of the following elements": goal setting and planning, organization of behaviors over time, flexibility, attention and memory systems such as working memory, and self-regulatory processes like self-monitoring. The editors note that fuzzy definitions still abound and different theories compete to explain EF development.
requirements: A definition must accommodate partial overlap across proposed element lists, since no unitary definition exists in the field
constraints: The field still lacks a unitary definition; the listed elements are shared by many but not all definitions
target_learners: learners across K-12 and higher education
examples: The volume organizes its three parts (theoretical frameworks, diagnostic groups, interventions) around this umbrella definition of EF processes
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Teaching metacognitive strategies that address executive function processes within a schoolwide curriculum
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: EF as how-and-when functions on equal footing with other cognitive domains, not a higher-order pinnacle
description: Denckla argues against hierarchical models that place executive function above other cognition. She concludes the EF domain "is not above other cognitive domains, not some reified and exalted higher-order pinnacle of cognition, not meta- but intra- and intercognitive," and proposes speaking of EF as encompassing how-and-when functions, colloquially getting your act together. She warns the meta- prefix disguises EF's developmental dynamics and ignores subcortical contributions, since EF develops from about 9 months of age into the fourth decade in looping interaction with other domains.
requirements: EF should be understood through systems-and-circuits brain analysis rather than hierarchical meta-levels
constraints: The account is a neuropsychological argument grounded in clinical observation and developmental literature, not a tested model
target_learners: children and adolescents with executive function difficulties
students with ADHD and learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: understanding executive function as action control (initiate, sustain, shift, inhibit)
recognizing EF's reciprocal interaction with language and other domains
examples: Denckla uses a cooking analogy: a meal requires both ingredients and recipes, since the how and when of EF is meaningless without reciprocal interaction with other cognitive and motor domains
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Teaching metacognitive strategies that address executive function processes within a schoolwide curriculum
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Translate executive function terminology into familiar educational language for cross-professional communication
description: Denckla recommends bridging the medical and educational perspectives by translating EF/EDF terminology into words familiar in special education. Professionals comfortable with EF terminology can communicate with education by "translating or analyzing EF into more familiar words like planning, organization, study skills, and self-monitoring/checking skills," terms that have existed in learning disabilities literature for decades. This translation lets brain-based and school-based professionals apply EF concepts without the formidable resonance of the clinical label.
requirements: Professionals must recognize which aspects of attention and memory (executive/selective attention, working memory) fall under the executive domain
constraints: The domains of attention and memory straddle brain-based and school-based understandings, making some splits hard to communicate across professions
target_learners: students with ADHD and learning disabilities served in schools
examples: Denckla notes organizational planning and working memory have long been recognized in special education under the names sequencing and short-term memory within IEPs
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Executive function as an umbrella term for goal-directed cognitive processes with five recurring elements
description: The volume's Part I introduction defines executive function as "an umbrella term for the complex cognitive processes that serve ongoing, goal-directed behaviors." Most definitions include many, but not all, of five elements: goal setting and planning, organization of behaviors over time, flexibility, attention and memory systems such as working memory, and self-regulatory processes such as self-monitoring. The editors note that fuzzy definitions still abound and different theories compete to explain EF development.
requirements: Definitions must specify which of the five elements they include, since no definition includes all of them
constraints: The field had not achieved a unitary definition of executive function at the time of publication
target_learners: students with learning disabilities and ADHD
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Executive function as 'how and when' functions on equal footing with other cognitive domains, not a higher-order pinnacle
description: Denckla argues against hierarchical models that place executive function above other cognitive domains, calling EF "not meta- but intra- and intercognitive." She proposes speaking of EF as encompassing "how and when" functions, analogous to 'where' and 'when' characterizations of perception, and criticizes the 'meta-' prefix of metacognition as disguising the developmental dynamics of EF and leading to neglect of subcortical contributions. EF develops in interactive, looping fashion with other cognitive domains from about 9 months of age into the fourth decade of life.
requirements: Descriptions of EF must account for its reciprocal interaction with language, memory, and motor domains rather than treating it as an overseer
constraints: The account is grounded in a systems-and-circuits analysis of the brain rather than theory-driven distinctions
target_learners: children and adolescents with executive function difficulties
students with ADHD and learning disabilities

article_title: The contribution of executive functions to creativity in children: What is the role of crystallized and fluid intelligence?
citation: Krumm, Gabriela Liliana; Arán Filippetti, Vanessa; Gutierrez Saez, Marisel Luisa. (2018). The contribution of executive functions to creativity in children: What is the role of crystallized and fluid intelligence?. Thinking Skills and Creativity. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2018.07.006
title: Executive functions support creativity differentially in children, with shifting central to the intelligence-creativity link
description: The article proposes a model in which creativity in children is supported differentially by distinct executive functions rather than uniformly, and in which crystallized intelligence affects creativity indirectly through shifting. The authors state that "EFs differently support creativity in children" and that SEM showed the Gc effect on creativity "was mediated by shifting". The model was tested with SEM on measures of working memory, inhibition and shifting alongside Gc, Gf and creativity in 209 children aged 8 to 13.
requirements: Requires measures of creativity, crystallized and fluid intelligence, and the three EF components (working memory, inhibition, shifting) to test the differential contributions
constraints: Findings concern children aged 8 to 13; the abstract notes most prior research focused on adult populations
examples: SEM analysis of 209 children's creativity, intelligence and EF measures testing mediation of the Gc-creativity relation by shifting
key_sources: Krumm, Gabriela Liliana; Arán Filippetti, Vanessa; Gutierrez Saez, Marisel Luisa. (2018). The contribution of executive functions to creativity in children: What is the role of crystallized and fluid intelligence?. Thinking Skills and Creativity. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2018.07.006

article_title: How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study
citation: Viterbori, P.; Usai, M. C.; Traverso, L.; De Franchis, V. (2015). How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study. https://hdl.handle.net/11567/813133
title: Early childhood mathematics education should include interventions targeting executive function
description: The article concludes that its longitudinal findings "empirically support interventions that target EF as an important component of early childhood mathematics education." Because preschool WM–flexibility predicted later math achievement, EF training is positioned as a worthwhile component of early math programs. The article presents this as an implication of its predictive results.
requirements: EF components such as working memory–flexibility should be measurable in preschool children
constraints: Support is predictive (longitudinal correlational), not a demonstration that EF training improves math achievement
examples: The study assessed six EF measures in 175 five-year-olds and tracked math achievement through Grades 1 and 3
key_sources: Viterbori, P.; Usai, M. C.; Traverso, L.; De Franchis, V. (2015). How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study. https://hdl.handle.net/11567/813133

article_title: Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity
citation: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/
title: Efklides' three-dimensional model of metacognition maps onto the generative and exploratory stages of creativity
description: The article adopts Efklides' distinction between three dimensions of metacognition: metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, and metacognitive abilities. Metacognitive knowledge is declarative knowledge including information about persons, strategies, tasks, and goals; metacognitive experiences refer to awareness and feelings during task implementation; metacognitive abilities are skills used to control cognition, including planning, regulation, and evaluation. The author argues these dimensions are engaged differently across creative stages: "Metacognitive experiences are, probably, more important in the generative stage than in the exploratory stage", while metacognitive knowledge is more influential in exploratory stages, and abilities are triggered during both stages.
requirements: Distinguishes metacognitive knowledge, experiences, and abilities as separate dimensions
constraints: The mapping of dimensions onto creative stages is the author's theoretical proposal, not a tested result
target_learning_goals: understanding how different metacognitive dimensions support idea generation versus evaluation
examples: The author proposes metacognitive experiences help identify attentional shifts during idea generation, particularly mind wandering
key_sources: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/

article_title: Interventions Shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4 to 12 Years Old
citation: Diamond Adele, Lee Kathleen. (2011). Interventions shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4–12 Years Old. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1204529
title: Improve EFs by continually challenging them within activities that also address emotional, social, and physical development rather than focusing narrowly on EFs alone
description: The review distills cross-program lessons: EFs must be continually challenged to see improvements, since groups assigned the same program without difficulty increasing show no EF gains. It concludes the most effective way to improve EFs and academic achievement is probably not to focus narrowly on EFs alone but to also address emotional, social, and physical development, as the four EF-enhancing curricula do.
requirements: Repeated practice with progressively increasing difficulty; even the best activity done rarely produces little benefit
constraints: Computer training tends to be short-duration as interest wanes and highest game levels are reached; after-school options cost money and are not possible for all families
target_learning_goals: executive functions: cognitive flexibility, inhibition, working memory
examples: Control groups playing the same training games without difficulty increasing did not show the same gains; the four curricula-based programs reduce classroom stress, cultivate joy and pride, and foster social bonding
key_sources: Diamond Adele, Lee Kathleen. (2011). Interventions shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4–12 Years Old. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1204529

article_title: Activities and Programs That Improve Children’s Executive Functions
citation: Diamond Adele. (2012). Activities and Programs That Improve Children's Executive Functions. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721412453722
title: Shared design features of school curricula shown to improve children's executive functions
description: The review identifies ten features shared by the two curricula empirically shown to improve children's EFs, Montessori and Tools of the Mind, and notes many also characterize PATHS and CSRP. The curricula "help children exercise their EFs and constantly challenge them to do so at higher levels" while also reducing classroom stress, rarely embarrassing a child, cultivating joy and self-confidence, using hands-on learning, accommodating different rates of progress, emphasizing character development and oral language, engaging children in teaching one another, and fostering social skills and bonding.
requirements: The curriculum must embed EF practice throughout the day in all activities rather than in a single isolated module, as the review says curricula shown to improve EFs do.
constraints: The review notes both Tools of the Mind and CSRP are meant to be used only with children aged 3 to 6, and no program shown to improve EFs has reported benefits in children older than 9 years.
target_learners: Preschool and early-elementary children (ages 3 to 6 for Tools of the Mind and CSRP)
target_learning_goals: Executive functions: inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and school readiness
examples: Disadvantaged preschool children randomly assigned to a CSRP Head Start class showed better EFs than controls at year end and continued to outperform controls in math and reading for the next 3 years, with academic gains mediated almost entirely through improved EFs (Li-Grining et al., 2011).
key_sources: Diamond Adele. (2012). Activities and Programs That Improve Children's Executive Functions. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721412453722

article_title: Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation
citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Effort regulation score: bias measure of metacognitive regulation of mental effort
description: The article's measure of metacognitive regulation of mental effort: after each Multi-Strategy Test version, learners retrospectively rated required mental effort ("How hard would you have had to work on this assignment to get a very good grade?") and invested mental effort ("How much effort did you actually make at the task right now?") on 9-point Likert-type scales. The authors "computed an effort regulation score by subtracting the required mental effort rating from the invested mental effort rating"; negative values indicate deficient regulation, values around zero or positive indicate optimal regulation. Extreme difference scores of +8 or -8 were treated as missing values. The measure deliberately references effort for the task's intended goals to relate regulation to task performance.
requirements: Ratings are administered retrospectively after task completion, because continuous monitoring during learning changes effort estimates and retrospective measures are argued to be more valid
constraints: Learners can score high even if their subjective experience of required effort differs from the objective effort actually required
target_learners: students aged about 10 years (5th and 6th grade)
target_learning_goals: measuring metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort
examples: Administered after both the MST Experimentation and MST Exam Preparation versions at pretest and posttest
key_sources: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x

article_title: Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning?
citation: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z
title: Taxonomy of effort constructs distinguishing task-imposed from voluntarily allocated effort
description: The commentary organizes the proliferating effort terminology along one axis: whether effort is imposed by the task or voluntarily allocated by the learner. Mental load, data-driven effort, and effort-by-complexity can be modelled purely cognitively, whereas mental effort, goal-driven effort, effort-by-allocation, and effort-by-need frustration — defined as "how strenuous or aversive a person experiences task execution" — all carry a motivational component. The article uses this taxonomy to diagnose where CLT and SRL accounts diverge.
requirements: Distinguishing task-imposed from learner-allocated constructs when measuring or discussing effort
constraints: The commentary notes there are no precise scientific definitions of effort; research traditions each use their own understanding of the construct
target_learners: learners in educational settings studying with instructional materials
target_learning_goals: understanding and regulating effort during learning and problem solving
examples: The commentary maps CLT's mental load/mental effort distinction onto Koriat et al.'s data-driven/goal-driven effort and Grund et al.'s effort-by-complexity/effort-by-allocation distinctions
key_sources: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z

article_title: Cognitive Load and Challenges in Self-regulation: An Introduction and Reflection on the Topical Collection
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Janssen, E. M., Waldeyer, J., & Stebner, F. (2025). Cognitive Load and Challenges in Self-regulation: An Introduction and Reflection on the Topical Collection. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10042-2
title: Grund et al. (2024) categorize mental effort by psychological sources: effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation
description: A review by Grund et al. (2024) introduces "a novel categorization of how to conceptualize effort based on its underlying psychological sources of experiencing and allocating mental effort: effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation." The authors argue that motivational and emotional factors shape both willingness to invest effort and whether effort is experienced as manageable or taxing, and call for including affective components when measuring cognitive mental effort.
requirements: Measurement of cognitive mental effort should consider its affective components
target_learners: learners working on effortful learning tasks
target_learning_goals: conceptualization and measurement of mental effort in learning
examples: The editorial recommends disentangling effort due to task complexity from effort due to need frustration, optimizing the first while minimizing the latter
key_sources: de Bruin, A. B. H., Janssen, E. M., Waldeyer, J., & Stebner, F. (2025). Cognitive Load and Challenges in Self-regulation: An Introduction and Reflection on the Topical Collection. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10042-2

article_title: Making the Executive ‘Function’ for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions
citation: Scerif, G., Blakey, E., Gattas, S., Hawes, Z., Howard, S., Merkley, R., O'Connor, R., & Simms, V. (2023). Making the Executive 'Function' for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09824-3
title: Four-mechanism taxonomy of EF–mathematics relationships: performance foe, learning foe, learning ally, explicit learning ally
description: The review proposes four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms by which EF relates to early mathematics. EF may be "a performance foe" (a constraint on demonstrating skills), "a learning foe" (learning mathematics is EF-demanding), "a learning ally" (EF challenge deepens processing of mathematical concepts), or "an explicit learning ally" (adult-guided EF challenge in play-based activities builds metacognitive appreciation of challenge). The taxonomy implies different intervention designs: reducing EF demands suits struggling older learners, whereas well-calibrated increasing EF challenge should facilitate transfer for beginning learners.
requirements: Explicit operationalisation of the mechanism by which EF and mathematics interact during learning, since differing relationships lead to different intervention designs
constraints: The review argues the performance-foe account may fit older struggling learners but that preschool evidence does not point in that direction; remediation for later difficulties is distinguished from laying foundations for all learners
target_learners: Preschool and early primary children beginning mathematics learning
target_learning_goals: Foundational numeracy and executive function co-development
examples: The review's dots-estimation game: keeping mathematical content within the child's range while adaptively increasing EF demands (shorter estimation time, mixed-colour dots) is hypothesised to make EF a learning ally
key_sources: Scerif, G., Blakey, E., Gattas, S., Hawes, Z., Howard, S., Merkley, R., O'Connor, R., & Simms, V. (2023). Making the Executive 'Function' for the Foundations of Mathematics: the Need for Explicit Theories of Change for Early Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09824-3

article_title: Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased?
citation: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9
title: Effort appraisals are a type of metacognitive judgment that may be prone to biases through heuristic cue utilization
description: The review proposes that mental effort appraisals function as metacognitive judgments—subjective assessments based on how a person thinks about their cognition rather than on the cognition itself. Like judgments of learning and confidence, they may rely on heuristic cues with varying diagnosticity and be prone to biases, yet still guide regulatory decisions. The review states that "effort appraisals are, in fact, a type of metacognitive judgment" and suggests "the possibility that also effort appraisals may hence be prone to biases, but nevertheless guide people's actions."
requirements: Effort appraisals must be treated as subjective measures requiring validation against objective effort indicators
target_learners: students performing learning or problem-solving tasks
adults and children across cognitive domains
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of cognitive effort investment during learning
key_sources: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9

article_title: Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models
citation: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2
title: Effort–certainty–performance conceptual framework (De Bruin et al., 2017)
description: The article describes a conceptual framework, attributed to De Bruin et al. (2017) and supported by Blissett et al. (2018), in which "mental effort directly influences diagnostic accuracy (performance) and also indirectly influences it through certainty (monitoring judgment)". It treats the mental effort–certainty relation as linear, an assumption the reanalysis challenges by finding a cubic relation. The reanalysis's logistic models tested the framework's suggested causal paths and found evidence favouring simplification to certainty alone predicting performance.
requirements: The framework as specified assumes a linear mental effort–certainty relation, which the article's reanalysis did not support
constraints: The reanalysis found evidence against the framework in its original form, favouring a model in which certainty alone predicts performance
examples: The reanalysis compared five logistic models (L0–L4) representing the framework, its simplification, extension, or revision
key_sources: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2

article_title: Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective
citation: Emely Hoch, Yael Sidi, Rakefet Ackerman, Vincent Hoogerheide, Katharina Scheiter. (2023). Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09779-5
title: Treat mental effort and difficulty self-reports as heuristic metacognitive appraisals rather than reliable reflections of cognitive load
description: The article argues that load-related self-reports should be interpreted through the metacognitive cue-utilization lens: like confidence judgments, they are inferential and "prone to misleading cues like other metacognitive judgments", so researchers and designers should not treat them as direct readouts of cognitive load. The principle follows from the finding that effort and difficulty appraisals track response time more strongly than confidence does, and predict success less strongly than difficulty and confidence appraisals.
requirements: Interpretation of effort/difficulty ratings should account for heuristic cues such as response time and item complexity rather than assuming direct correspondence with cognitive load
constraints: The article notes the distinction between cognitive load types, and germane load as a category, is under debate; its findings concern classic global mental effort and difficulty scales
target_learners: Adult problem-solvers in online reasoning experiments (Prolific participants)
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of self-reported cognitive load in learning research and instructional design evaluation
examples: Across three experiments, the authors conclude these findings "challenge the accepted notion that mental effort appraisals can serve as reliable reflections of cognitive load"
key_sources: Emely Hoch, Yael Sidi, Rakefet Ackerman, Vincent Hoogerheide, Katharina Scheiter. (2023). Comparing Mental Effort, Difficulty, and Confidence Appraisals in Problem-Solving: A Metacognitive Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09779-5

article_title: The timing of executive function development is associated with growth in math achievement from preschool through second grade
citation: Sammy F. Ahmed, Janelle J. Montroy, Lori E. Skibbe, Ryan P. Bowles, & Frederick J. Morrison. (2022). The Timing of Executive Function Development is Associated with Growth in Math Achievement from Preschool through Second Grade. Manuscript in-press at Learning and Instruction. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3814-2955
title: Three-class classification of EF developmental timing: early, intermediate, and later developers
description: The article uses a previously established growth mixture modeling (GMM) classification in which young children follow distinct EF growth trajectories relative to peers. Children were classified as developing EF early, intermediate, or later: "24% of children were classified as developing EF “early”", while "Almost half (i.e., 48%) of children were “intermediate developers”" and 28% were later developers. Early developers start preschool with higher EF and grow rapidly across preschool; intermediate developers start lower and grow more slowly; later developers start comparable to the intermediate group but show minimal preschool growth, with major EF gains occurring later. The present study used these classifications as multigroup predictors of math growth.
requirements: EF scores grouped into six-month developmental windows between preschool and second grade and parameterized with an exponential growth model before GMM classification
constraints: Acceleration and deceleration rates were constrained to equality across trajectory classes, so trajectories differed in timing rather than variation; class membership was implicitly treated as directly observed and should be interpreted with caution
target_learners: children in preschool through second grade
examples: In the present study's sample, 24% were early, 48% intermediate, and 28% later EF developers; a 3-step robustness check produced the same patterns of results
key_sources: Sammy F. Ahmed, Janelle J. Montroy, Lori E. Skibbe, Ryan P. Bowles, & Frederick J. Morrison. (2022). The Timing of Executive Function Development is Associated with Growth in Math Achievement from Preschool through Second Grade. Manuscript in-press at Learning and Instruction. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3814-2955

article_title: A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect
citation: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y
title: Effort-based tutoring (EBT): adaptive problem selection and pedagogical moves inferred from correctness, help requests and time
description: EBT is Wayang Outpost's pedagogical decision-making model. It "adapts problem selection depending on the effort exerted by a student on a practice activity based on three different dimensions of student behavior: attempts to solve a problem, help requested, and time to answer". It defines a region of expected behavior per problem from historical log data, infers a most-likely student state (e.g., mastery without effort, hint abuse, low effort), and selects pedagogical and affective/motivational moves accordingly (Table 1). The authors contrast it with BKT and IRT, claiming it models cognitive, affective and metacognitive states together and captures inherent item difficulty beyond the required procedure.
requirements: Expected values E(Ii), E(Hi), E(Ti) and delta thresholds per problem estimated from accumulated student-problem interaction data across years
Content availability and classroom-management constraints such as minimum problems and maximum review time per topic
constraints: The authors state they do not claim a non-Bayesian approach is superior to Bayesian knowledge tracing, as further studies would be needed
EBT is used for decisions within a knowledge unit, while BKT-style mastery estimation is used at the topic level
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: mathematics problem solving on standardized-test items
examples: Table 1 maps nine observed behavior patterns (incorrect answers, hints, time) to decisions such as increase, maintain or reduce problem difficulty and affective responses like praising effort or deemphasizing immediate success
key_sources: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y

article_title: “How Did I Do?”: Giving learners effective and affective feedback
citation: Howard, N. R. (2021). "How Did I Do?": Giving learners effective and affective feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09874-2
title: Design digital feedback experiences so they are efficient and offer affective benefits to students and instructors
description: The article argues that future efforts should "ensure students and instructors are engaged in an efficient feedback experience that offers affective benefits in digital learning spaces". It treats feedback in digital learning as something that should serve both efficiency and affect, positioning Borup et al.'s work as "a critical anchor" for such efforts. The principle is stated as a design goal rather than tested here.
requirements: Feedback delivery in digital learning spaces must attend to both efficiency and affective benefits for students and instructors, as the article states.
target_learning_goals: effective and affective feedback experiences in online and blended learning
examples: The article offers this as a goal for future efforts building on Borup et al.'s (2015) examination of feedback perceptions in blended learning.
key_sources: Howard, N. R. (2021). "How Did I Do?": Giving learners effective and affective feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09874-2

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Synthesis: Examining the Academic Impacts of Feedback on Student Achievement
citation: Nalline S. Baliram & Jeffrey J. Youde. (2018). A Meta-analytic Synthesis: Examining the academic impacts of feedback on student achievement. International Dialogues on Education, 5(2), 76-90. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2198-5944
title: Effective feedback should be clear, age-appropriate, content-specific, timely, and of high quality
description: The article adopts Brookhart's (2008) criteria for effective feedback: it "should be clear, age -appropriate, content specific, timely, and of high quality." Effective feedback focuses on the task, process, and self-regulation, is descriptive, and includes praise along with constructive criticism. The meta-analysis results align with these recommendations, with content-specific feedback showing the largest moderator effect.
requirements: Feedback must be relevant to the students' reflection and learning process, and teachers must be aware of students' abilities, learning needs, and interests when deciding how and what feedback to give.
constraints: Feedback that is no longer relevant to current or future content may have diminished effectiveness; timely feedback within minutes of task completion may be unrealistic in larger classrooms.
examples: The article's moderator coding classified data sets as content-specific, praise, or objective feedback; content-specific examples included written comments related to the task and visual and oral performance feedback.
key_sources: Nalline S. Baliram & Jeffrey J. Youde. (2018). A Meta-analytic Synthesis: Examining the academic impacts of feedback on student achievement. International Dialogues on Education, 5(2), 76-90. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2198-5944

article_title: Effect of classroom physical activity breaks on learning behaviors and academic achievements in university students: a systematic review.
citation: Deng Qianting; Wu Chongyun; Yang Luodan. (2026). Effect of classroom physical activity breaks on learning behaviors and academic achievements in university students: a systematic review. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-026-01936-7
title: Effort-recovery and physiological mechanisms account for effects of classroom activity breaks on learning
description: The review explains the benefits of activity breaks via the effort-recovery model, which 'emphasizes the dynamic and reversible nature of fatigue' alleviated by restorative activities, plus proposed physiological mechanisms: BDNF upregulation supporting synaptic plasticity and memory consolidation, acute increases in arousal and alertness, enhanced neurotransmitter dynamics (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin), reduced sympathetic activity with enhanced parasympathetic modulation, and improved executive function and brain network connectivity.
requirements: Proposed to operate when task demands are alleviated by restorative activities such as appropriate rest or physical exercise
constraints: The review presents these mechanisms as proposed explanations, not as directly tested within the included studies
examples: The review cites evidence that structured exercise breaks boosted vitality with effects sustained up to 20 min, while another study found emotional improvements diminishing within 30 min.
key_sources: Deng Qianting; Wu Chongyun; Yang Luodan. (2026). Effect of classroom physical activity breaks on learning behaviors and academic achievements in university students: a systematic review. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-026-01936-7

article_title: Is there sufficient evidence for the association between executive dysfunction and academic performance in adolescents with major depressive disorder?: a systematic review.
citation: Urbańska-Grosz J, Walkiewicz M, Sitek EJ. (2023). Is there sufficient evidence for the association between executive dysfunction and academic performance in adolescents with major depressive disorder?: a systematic review. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-023-02275-9
title: Executive functions as a multidimensional construct whose components relate differently to educational achievement across developmental stages
description: The review organises executive functions (EF) as a multi-dimensional construct encompassing prioritising, planning, initiating, maintaining and inhibiting goal-directed activity, monitoring performance, coordinating multiple activities and modifying strategy. It frames EF components as differentially important across education stages: inhibitory control matters at early school age, while planning multi-step activity gains importance once basic academic skills are mastered. The authors write that "EF as a multi-dimensional construct enable us to prioritise, plan, initiate, maintain and inhibit goal-directed activity, as well as monitor our performance, coordinate the performance of multiple activities, and modify our strategy".
requirements: Assessment must cover multiple EF components, as no single test captures all aspects; the review notes none of the included studies assessed all aspects of executive functions
constraints: Executive skills continue to evolve up to early adulthood, and the evolution of hot executive skills such as affective decision-making is unlikely to be linear, complicating study of EF in depressed adolescents
target_learning_goals: self-regulation strategies for classroom and individual study
examples: The review used this framework to classify the five included studies' measures into planning/decision-making, inhibitory control, working memory/attention, set-shifting and meta-tasking columns (Table 2), noting meta-tasking was never assessed
key_sources: Urbańska-Grosz J, Walkiewicz M, Sitek EJ. (2023). Is there sufficient evidence for the association between executive dysfunction and academic performance in adolescents with major depressive disorder?: a systematic review. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-023-02275-9

article_title: The Effects of Training in Timing and Rhythm on Reading Achievement
citation: Gordon E. Taub, Philip J. Lazarus. (2012). The Effects Of Training In Timing And Rhythm On Reading Achievement. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, Volume 5, Number 4. http://www.cluteinstitute.com/
title: Efficient cognitive processing account of timing-training reading gains
description: The article proposes that the observed reading gains arise not from new academic knowledge but from more efficient processing of existing knowledge: "participants did not acquire more academic knowledge, however, experimental group participants appeared to process their acquired knowledge m ore efficiently". It situates this within fluency theory, contrasting an automaticity account with a prosody account, and lists fluency's primary components as accuracy in decoding, automaticity in word recognition, and appropriate use of prosodic features. Timing and rhythm are positioned as underlying both automaticity and prosody in reading.
requirements: Improvement is attributed to processing efficiency of already-acquired knowledge rather than direct academic instruction
constraints: The account is the authors' hypothesis, not a tested mechanism in this study
examples: The authors use the WJ III Reading Fluency task of quickly judging sentences such as whether a fish lives on land as requiring efficient mental processing rather than new learning
key_sources: Gordon E. Taub, Philip J. Lazarus. (2012). The Effects Of Training In Timing And Rhythm On Reading Achievement. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, Volume 5, Number 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1073174

article_title: Using Facebook as a LMS?
citation: Arabacioglu, T. & Akar-Vural, R. (2014). Using Facebook as a LMS?. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Effective Teaching Scale (Ginns & Ellis 2009) adapted to Turkish
description: The study adapted the 'Evaluating the quality of e-learning at the degree level in the student experience of blended learning' scale by Ginns and Ellis (2009) with required permissions. The scale is composed of a total of twenty-eight items and six sub scales: good teaching, Clear Goals and Standards, appropriate assessment, appropriate workload, e-learning and generic skills. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses confirmed the six-factor structure as a model, with Cronbach alpha of .91 for the whole scale.
requirements: Adaptation study with required permissions from original authors
constraints: Two subscales (assessment and appropriate workload) showed low reliability (α=.51 and α=.50)
target_learning_goals: Evaluating quality of e-learning and effective teaching
examples: Used to compare perceptions of effective teaching between Facebook and Adobe Connect groups
key_sources: Arabacioglu, T. & Akar-Vural, R. (2014). Using Facebook as a LMS?. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1022959

article_title: Effective Professional Development of Teachers: A Guide to Actualizing Inclusive Schooling
citation: Nishimura, T. (2014). Effective Professional Development of Teachers: A Guide to Actualizing Inclusive Schooling. International Journal of Whole Schooling, 10(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1055365
title: Effective professional development is characterized by individualization, coaching, collaboration, and daily embedding.
description: The article identifies four qualities of effective professional development drawn from Bull and Buechler (1997) and Desimone (2009). These include that PD should "be individualized and school based, utilizes coaching and other follow up procedures, engages in collaboration, and embeds practices into the daily lives of teachers." This contrasts with the traditional "sit and get" one-time in-service model, which relies solely on participants to implement new knowledge individually and often does not sustain change.
requirements: Professional development must be tailored to individual teacher needs and school context rather than delivered as generic one-time events.
constraints: The collaborative approach to professional development requires more time and effort than traditional models.
target_learning_goals: Implementing and sustaining inclusive education practices
examples: The article's IPD study operationalized these qualities through individualized coaching sessions tailored to each teacher's identified needs across five core areas.
key_sources: Nishimura, T. (2014). Effective Professional Development of Teachers: A Guide to Actualizing Inclusive Schooling. International Journal of Whole Schooling, 10(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1016781

article_title: Preschoolers' Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22
citation: Ackerman, D. J., & Friedman-Krauss, A. H. (2017). Preschoolers’ Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22. https://doi.org/10.1002/ets2.12148
title: Executive function can be characterized by three-category and four-category models
description: The report describes two structural models of EF. One theory collapses EF-related skills into three categories: inhibitory control (also referred to as self-control or impulse control), cognitive or mental flexibility (or attention switching or set shifting), and working memory (the ability to hold information in one’s mind and use it). Another related theory characterizes EF as a domain with four distinct regions: attentional control, cognitive flexibility, goal setting, and information processing. The first two categories overlap with the three-category model, while goal setting is defined as reasoning and formulating a plan of sequential steps toward reaching a specific end point, and information processing is the extent to which an individual can organize thoughts and weed through bits of information.
requirements: The processes within each domain are highly integrated, and all domains are bidirectionally related and must work together for optimal functioning.
constraints: Certain tasks will demand higher levels of input from specific EF domains.
key_sources: Ackerman, D. J., & Friedman-Krauss, A. H. (2017). Preschoolers’ Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22. https://doi.org/10.1002/ets2.12148

article_title: Preschoolers' Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22
citation: Ackerman, D. J., & Friedman-Krauss, A. H. (2017). Preschoolers’ Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22. https://doi.org/10.1002/ets2.12148
title: Executive function can be divided into hot and cool categories based on emotional involvement
description: The report describes a theory that divides EF into hot and cool categories. Tasks that involve hot EF typically involve some type of emotional component, such as a reward or fear. Conversely, tasks that involve cool EF are considered to be decontextualized and thus more emotionally neutral. This division is supported by research finding a strong positive correlation between preschoolers’ inhibitory control and emotion regulation, as well as a positive impact of a promised reward on inhibitory control.
requirements: The hot/cool distinction makes sense in light of research connecting inhibitory control with emotion regulation and reward effects.
constraints: Even healthy adults’ capacity to focus, exercise self-control, and use working memory can be impaired in situations that produce anxiety or other negative emotions.
key_sources: Ackerman, D. J., & Friedman-Krauss, A. H. (2017). Preschoolers’ Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22. https://doi.org/10.1002/ets2.12148

article_title: Mathematics-Related Competence of Early Childhood Teachers Visiting a Continuous Professional Development Course: An Intervention Study
citation: Julia Bruns, Lars Eichen, Hedwig Gasteiger. (2017). Mathematics-related Competence of Early Childhood Teachers Visiting a Continuous Professional Development Course: An Intervention Study. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development, 19(3), 76-93. MERGA.
title: Effective professional development courses on early childhood mathematics should be long-lasting, competence-oriented and foster a broad understanding of mathematics
description: Based on a synthesis of research on professional development, the article states that "effective professional development courses on early childhood mathematics education are long lasting, competence-oriented and foster a broad understanding of mathematics related to several content areas." Long-lasting means continuous rather than one-day training, with a suggested minimum duration of 53 hours; competence-oriented means developing knowledge, observation tools and evaluation criteria rather than only presenting hands-on materials; broad understanding means drawing a versatile picture of mathematics beyond counting and cardinality.
requirements: A minimum duration of 53 hours based on a meta-analysis by Yoon, Duncan, Lee, Scarloss, and Shapley (2007); combining presence and practical phases.
examples: The EmMa course was designed along these characteristics: it lasts one year (~100 hours), combines presence and practical phases, and addresses content areas including number and operations, geometry, and measurement.
key_sources: Julia Bruns, Lars Eichen, Hedwig Gasteiger. (2017). Mathematics-related Competence of Early Childhood Teachers Visiting a Continuous Professional Development Course: An Intervention Study. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development, 19(3), 76-93. MERGA. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1163878

article_title: Riding toward better math: executive functions mediate the link between horseback activities and children's mathematical achievement.
citation: Almutairi Seham. (2026). Riding toward better math: executive functions mediate the link between horseback activities and children's mathematical achievement. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04596-1
title: Executive Functioning Scale (EFS), Arabic-adapted parent-report instrument
description: The Executive Functioning Scale is a 52-item parent-report instrument rated on a 5-point Likert scale that captures both "cool" (cognitive) and "hot" (emotional–motivational) dimensions of executive functioning, yielding five subscale scores and a Global Executive Functioning Index. In this study it was translated into Arabic following WHO guidelines, achieving "high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.88)" and supporting its applicability for children aged 7–9 in Arabic-speaking contexts. It served as the sole EF measure, with the five domains indicating a latent EF construct in the SEM.
requirements: Parent informants complete the 52 items; the instrument is distributed under a CC-BY 4.0 open-access license permitting translation with citation
constraints: Parent-reported ratings capture everyday executive performance rather than maximal capacity under laboratory conditions; single-informant design may introduce rater-specific variance
target_learning_goals: assessment of everyday executive functions (organization and planning, working memory, emotion regulation, self-control, motivation)
examples: Used as the sole EF measure in the SEM, with the five domains as latent indicators
key_sources: Almutairi Seham. (2026). Riding toward better math: executive functions mediate the link between horseback activities and children's mathematical achievement. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04596-1

article_title: Assessing the Quality of Narrative Feedback in Entrustable Professional Activities Using the EFeCT Feedback Scoring Tool.
citation: Lee R., Dhami N., Gibson W., Hamza D. M., Oswald A. E., Moffat M. (2026). Assessing the Quality of Narrative Feedback in Entrustable Professional Activities Using the EFeCT Feedback Scoring Tool. The Clinical Teacher 23(1): e70295. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70295
title: EFeCT Feedback Scoring Tool
description: The Evaluation of Feedback Captured Tool (EFeCT) scores written feedback on workplace assessments against five criteria considered essential components of high-quality feedback, each scored 1 (met) or 0 (not met), yielding a 0–5 total where higher scores indicate higher quality. It "allocates points for the task being performed ('where am I going'), how the learner did ('how am I going') and what was done well or needs improvement and how it was done well or can be improved ('where to next')", plus a point for context. Criteria are not hierarchical, and teaching-only comments or encounter logs rank 0. In this study it was used by three evaluators to score EPA narrative feedback.
requirements: Requires written narrative feedback on the assessment form to score; teaching-only comments with no reference to learner performance rank 0.
constraints: Originally developed for programme-level evaluation of narrative feedback quality in assessment forms, not originally for faculty development.
target_learning_goals: quality of formative narrative feedback on clinical performance
examples: Three evaluators used the EFeCT tool to score 748 EPA observations, resolving scoring differences by consensus.
key_sources: Lee R., Dhami N., Gibson W., Hamza D. M., Oswald A. E., Moffat M. (2026). Assessing the Quality of Narrative Feedback in Entrustable Professional Activities Using the EFeCT Feedback Scoring Tool. The Clinical Teacher 23(1): e70295. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70295
